# Saṁvarajātaka (Ja 462)

**ID:** Ja 462
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (Pali):** Saṁvarajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Prince Saṁvara

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Saṁvarajātaka* (Ja 462) is a canonical Jātaka story preserved in the Pali Tipiṭaka [SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional framing of its commentary edited by Fausböll, the Buddha delivered the tale while dwelling at Jetavana in reference to a monk who had abandoned his striving [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887]. In the story of the past, King Saṁvara is identified with the formerly slack monk, Prince Uposatha with Sāriputta, the other royal brothers with the elders of the order, the retinue with the Buddha's assembly, and the wise counsellor-minister with the Bodhisatta [Fausböll 1887].

In Burmese Buddhist literature, the 15th-century monk-poet Raṭṭhasāra (born 1468 at Ratanapura) composed well-known poetical renderings of several Jātakas, including the *Saṁvarajātaka*, the *Bhūridattajātaka*, and the *Hatthipālajātaka* [Ray 1946]. As recorded by the Burmese chronicler Paññāsāmī, these poetic compositions on religious subjects attracted censure from more conservative monastic critics [Ray 1946].

According to DharmaNexus, verses and prose segments of the *Saṁvarajātaka* share substantial internal text reuse with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (matching both volume 4, segments 4.1–9.4, and volume 7) [DharmaNexus]. In cross-language alignments, DharmaNexus detects matches with the Chinese translation of the *Bieyi za ahan jing* (T 100) and the Tibetan *Ārya-sūryagarbha-nāma-vaipulya-sūtra* (D 257), though SuttaCentral does not register curated parallels for this text [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
